title: India's Monsoon Has Delivered 42% Less Rain Than Normal. Farmers Are Running Out of Time.
excerpt: Kharif sowing is down 23%, cotton acreage has cratered 35%, and a Super El Niño is building. Here's what the worst June rainfall in over a decade means for food prices, markets, and the families NRIs send money home to.
body:
June is ending with India's monsoon in crisis. As of June 29, the country has received 42 per cent less rainfall than the seasonal average — a deficit that has widened steadily since mid-month and shows no sign of closing. The India Meteorological Department's own models, along with international forecasters, are now converging on a sobering conclusion: this will be India's weakest monsoon in 11 years, and it could get considerably worse.

The culprit is El Niño. A powerful warming of the central and eastern Pacific Ocean, declared just weeks ago, is actively suppressing the monsoon's moisture-laden winds. In previous dry years — 2023 is the closest analogue — a positive Indian Ocean Dipole acted as a counterweight, pulling extra moisture toward the subcontinent and salvaging near-normal rainfall even under El Niño's drag. This year, the Indian Ocean is locked in neutral. There is no cushion.

The Busan-based APEC Climate Centre projects rainfall during July through September — the monsoon's remaining months — to be 53.8 per cent below normal, the largest shortfall forecast anywhere in Asia. Even the IMD's relatively conservative estimate pegs the season at just 90 per cent of the long-period average of 86.86 cm, the worst since 2015.

## The Fields Are Already Telling the Story

The rain deficit is not an abstraction. Farmers have planted summer-sown crops on just 18.27 million hectares as of June 25, nearly 23 per cent less than the same point last year, according to the Ministry of Agriculture. The shortfall is staggering across every major crop:

- **Soybean acreage has collapsed 65 per cent** — from 19.97 million hectares to 6.92 million hectares
- **Cotton is down 35 per cent**, to 2.97 million hectares from 4.54 million hectares
- **Groundnut is down 42 per cent**, to 8.87 million hectares from 15.29 million hectares
- **Rice transplanting is down 25 per cent**, to 2.58 million hectares from 3.44 million hectares
- **Arhar (pigeon peas)**, a staple protein source, has dropped 58 per cent from 8.45 to 3.56 million hectares

Some regions have been hit far harder than the national average. The rainfall deficit in parts of central India and the Deccan — which accounts for about 90 per cent of India's soybean and sugarcane crop, 80 per cent of its cotton, and 70 per cent of its pulses — runs as high as 92 per cent. Nashik, the heart of India's onion country and a politically salient crop because of its outsized impact on household budgets, has received just 16 per cent of its normal June rainfall.



> **"Farmers have planted summer-sown crops on just 18.27 million hectares as of June 25, nearly 23 per cent less than the same point last year, according to the Ministry of Agriculture."**


## The Government Is Planning for the Worst

Farm Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan chaired an emergency meeting with state-level agriculture ministers last week, acknowledging the scale of the problem. The government has drawn up contingency plans for over 300 districts deemed vulnerable to monsoon failure. Of these, 111 have been classified as high priority — districts where less than a quarter of farmland has irrigation — and another 76 as medium priority.

States have been advised to encourage farmers in rainfed areas to shift to short-duration, less water-intensive crops such as pulses, millets, and oilseeds. The government has also directed states to repair ponds, check dams, and other water-harvesting infrastructure.


![Indian Ocean Dipole — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f6/Sstanom_199711_krig.jpg)


The advice is pragmatic but it is also an admission: India's farm economy remains structurally exposed to rainfall. Nearly half of the country's farmland lacks irrigation, and roughly half its 1.4 billion people depend on agriculture for their livelihood.

## What NRIs Should Watch

The monsoon is not just an agricultural event. It is an economic one.

**Food prices are the first transmission channel.** Poor rainfall routinely triggers price spikes in onions, pulses, and vegetables — commodities that are staples for the families NRIs send remittances to. If the deficit persists through July, which is the most critical month for sowing and accounts for 32 per cent of seasonal rainfall, analysts warn inflation could spike toward 5.5 per cent, up from April's 3.48 per cent.

**Markets are already reacting.** The Nifty 50 fell 0.46 per cent on Monday, pausing its longest winning streak of 2026. The auto index dropped 2.1 per cent on fears that a weak monsoon would suppress demand for two-wheelers, entry-level cars, and tractors — products that depend heavily on rural purchasing power. Analysts at SMC Global noted that "only a pickup in July could revive optimism, given its implications for inflation, demand, and sectors such as autos and consumer goods."

**Rural incomes will be squeezed.** For millions of Indian families, the kharif harvest is the primary annual income event. A failed or diminished harvest means lower purchasing power, higher debt, and greater dependence on remittances from abroad.

There is some reassurance in the buffer stocks. Government warehouses hold record levels of rice — 15 per cent more than a year ago at the start of June. Wheat stocks are also ample. This means India is unlikely to face an outright food crisis, but prices for vegetables, oilseeds, and pulses — which do not enjoy the same buffer — could move sharply.

## What Comes Next

The IMD is scheduled to release its July forecast on Tuesday. July is the monsoon's wettest month and the last realistic window for farmers to sow most kharif crops. If rainfall remains 30 per cent or more below normal through the first half of July, the planting window will effectively close for cotton, soybean, and most pulses.

The FAO has separately warned that this El Niño could be one of the strongest in decades, arriving at a moment when global food systems are already under pressure from the disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz. For India, the convergence of a weak monsoon, a strong El Niño, and continuing Middle East-driven supply chain stress represents a triple threat that will test the resilience of its agricultural economy through the rest of the year.

For the diaspora, it is a reminder that the most consequential economic force in India is still the same one it has always been: the rain.
